subsubtopic: PROPOSED STUDY BY COMMITTEE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 to seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. In light of the fact the Urban Development Institute states that the shortage of reasonable cost housing in the urban centres of Canada has reached the proportions of a major social tragedy, I move:
That this House order that a standing committee of this House, known as housing and urban affairs, be set up to study matters which fall under the jursidiction of the Department of Housing and Urban Affairs, due to the fact that in some of the major cities of Canada only 4 per cent of the population can afford to buy a new house because of the outrageous cost and prices of same.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask leave to present a motion under Standing Order 43, and I hope that before there are automatic noes from the other side hon. members will listen to the reasonableness of my proposal. In view of the fact it would assist in settling the present postal dispute if parliament were to declare itself on the basic issue, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard):
That the question of amending the Public Service Staff Relations Act to provide for the classification of positions in the federal public service to be subject to collective bargaining, and particularly to grievance and arbitration, be referred forthwith to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subsubtopic: DECLINE IN DAIRY EXPORTS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave of the House to move a motion under Standing Order 43. The urgent and pressing necessity arises out of the continuing decline in our cheese, butter and other dairy exports to the United Kingdom and other European countries as a result of the expansion of the EEC. Therefore, if consent is given, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk):
That the Standing Committee of this House on Agriculture be instructed forthwith to examine the methods by which the drastic decline in Canada's dairy exports to Britain and the EEC countries may be halted, the effects of this decline on Canada's farmers and balance of payments position, and the possibility of finding alternative markets for dairy products.

speechtext:

The government is not on the verge of announcing price and wage controls, but we have stated repeatedly that it is something for which we have made contingency plans and which we are prepared to envisage when the time comes. Perhaps this committee which is to be set up by the House of Commons will indicate to us its views on that timing.

speechtext:
As I understand the suggestions that have been made by the hon. member for Peace River and the
Food Prices Committee
hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, there will be discussions to consider certain aspects of the motion before the House. I assume that these discussions will take place, but for the time being we will proceed with consideration of the motion before us.

speakeroldname: Mr. lames A. McGrath (St. lohn's East):
subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today is very similar to a motion placed on the order paper by the government in 1966 calling for the setting up at that time of a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons. I listened with great interest to the speech by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) in leading off the debate, but I am sorry to say that I found nothing new in what he had to say. His remarks were very similar to the speech made by the government representative in 1966 when a similar motion was introduced.
I was impressed, however, with the very excellent speech by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), and I might say that as a consequence of his intervention we now have before us a much more workable proposition, which hopefully will end up in the establishment of a much more workable committee. I listened as well with great interest, as I always try to do, to the speech by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). She has established herself in this House as an articulate and dedicated spokesman on consumer affairs. Hon. members of the government would do well to pay more attention to the remarks of the hon. member for V ancouver-Kingsway.
As I have said, this is not the first time that we have had a proposition like this put before us. I have already referred to the joint Senate and House of Commons committee set up in 1966 on April 21. This committee was given terms of reference almost identical to those we have before us today. Indeed, the terms of reference were identical to those of the committee that the government proposed to set up before the amendment placed before the House by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham was accepted last night.
It is interesting to look at the workings of that 1966 committee. As I say, it was set up in April of 1966. Its terms of reference were changed from the original consumer credit study to enable the committee to look into food prices. It submitted what was termed a progress report, which was in fact its final report, on April 25,1967. The committee met on 59 different occasions in the city of Ottawa between September 28, 1966 and February 1967. In addition, the committee was constituted into two subcommittees in order to facilitate its work. It went across the country holding public hearings in 12 of the principal cities of Canada and the major recommendation to come out of that committee, as is a matter of record, was the establishment of the department of consumer affairs.
We then had the Senate committee on poverty which also did excellent work. It was set up on November 26, 1968 and submitted its report in the fall of 1970. This was a study of poverty in Canada, but anybody who has read the report and followed the deliberations of that committee will know it had to concern itself with the general

January 19, 1973
Food Prices Committee
proposition of the cost of food as it related to poverty in Canada. The two are interrelated.
Going back to 1966, we saw the establishment of a royal commission by the governments of the three prairie provinces to look into food prices. This committee, after exhaustive studies, issued its report in March, 1968. It, too, is a matter of record. About the same time a royal commission was at work in my own province of Newfoundland, again examining the high cost of living and the cost of food. Then, there was another senate committee study, undertaken by the Senate Committee on Finance. It was empowered by the other place to look into the problems of growth, employment and price stability. The report of that committee is now a matter of record and it contains certain precise recommendations in line with its terms of reference.
Of course, we cannot forget for a moment the late and unlamented Prices and Incomes Commission which was established by the present government as a move to hold the line on inflation. We hear little now about the Prices and Incomes Commission and one wonders what happened to the very substantial organization which was put together as a result of the establishment of that commission. I understand that some parts of this organization are still in existence within the government structure. Perhaps the services of those parts may be very usefully called upon to assist this committee when it embarks upon its study.
I refer to the establishment of these committees and commissions to underline my central point, and that is the advisability of another study at this particular time. Here again I refer and defer to my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, although in doing so I have very serious reservations about just exactly what this committee of the House can hope to achieve, especially in light of the statement which was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) yesterday at the Federal-Provincial Conference simultaneous to the debate in this House on the setting up of this committee. The minister referred to the fact that he could see no improvement in the general situation so far as increases in food prices in Canada were concerned.
That utterance by the Minister of Finance was well stated today by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and leads us to question the motivation of the government in setting up this committee. If the government hopes to be able to sweep the problem under the carpet or have it pigeon-holed in that place where all similar committee studies, reports and recommendations are placed, then it does not have a full appreciation of the constitution of this parliament.
The House of Commons and the members of this place are not prepared, notwithstanding what the Minister of Finance may have had to say yesterday, to see this matter become the subject of pigeon-holding, or to see the deliberations of this committee swept under the carpet. Neither are the members of this House, if I may say so, prepared to see a situation similar to that which we had in 1966 when the committee of the Senate and the House of Commons was set up. I do not think the members of this House are prepared to support what could very well turn out to be, if the government has its way, one big junket across

the country for the members of this House. I do not think the members of this House are prepared for that, and neither, if I may say so, are the people of the country prepared to accept it.
There is sufficient data and there have been sufficient studies made, and I think one of the principal objectives of this committee should be to compile the principal recommendations of all of the committees to which I have just referred, because even though they may have been set up a few years ago, their findings and recommendations are still very relevant to the present situation we have in Canada. This is a serious problem, one that is far too serious to be swept under the carpet or to be pigeonholed after a long study by a Commons committee. This is serious because the people of Canada who are suffering the most today from inflation and from an increase in the cost of living are those on lower incomes, on middle incomes and those on fixed incomes; the poor, the working poor and our old age pensioners. We cannot afford to let too much time go by without addressing ourselves to this most serious problem facing our country today.
I happen to come from a province which enjoys the rather dubious distinction of having the highest per capita cost of living in the country and the lowest per capita income in the country. What has happened since this government came into office? About two years ago, we saw the government move to freeze freight rates. The consequence of their failure to do so has been nine increases in freight rates in two years. Every time the railways increase their freight rates, there is a concomitant increase in the cost of living, because an increase in freight rates must be passed on to the consumer who must ultimately pay the cost. Notwithstanding repeated pleas to the government to place an immediate freeze on freight rates, we are on the threshold of having further increases in freight rates. These increases are contributing to the high cost of living we have in the Atlantic provinces and all across Canada, for that matter. They are contributing substantially to the hardships we are imposing upon the poor, those on lower incomes and those on fixed incomes.
While I was encouraged by the reference in the Speech from the Throne to a conference the government proposes to convene with the five regions of the country and their provincial governments, on the whole area of freight rates and the influence freight rates have on the cost of living, I believe the problem is serious enough for the government to take steps now to bring a measure before this House which would place an immediate freeze on freight rates. In that way, the government would be demonstrating its good will and the fact that it is genuinely concerned about this matter. With the constitution of this parliament, who knows how long it will be before such a conference, badly needed as it is, can in fact take place?
Therefore, because of the urgency of the matter, because this is a serious situation, because it has been the subject of parliamentary committee studies before, because it has been the subject of study by royal commissions across the country and by provincial commissions, and in fact because we feel the matter has been studied sufficiently and is an urgent one, and in order to ensure that the committee will conduct itself in light of the urgen-
January 19, 1973

cy of the situation and report promptly to the House, I propose to place an amendment before the House.
I move, therefore, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer):
That the motion be amended by inserting therein, next after the third paragraph thereof, the following:
"That the said committee shall make its final report and recommendations within the three months next following its appointment.''

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is the first time I rise in this House other than at the oral questions period, I should like, first of all, to congratulate you and your Deputy (Mr. McCleave) on your appointment to your respective posts.

Mr. Speaker, since yesterday I have been listening to the various remarks which have been made on the matter of the special committee of the House on food prices. I have been trying to thread my way through the rather tortuous logic. I could assume that the tortuous logic came from all quarters of the House, but we have had a very good sample of it from the benches immediately to my right. On the one hand, I hear that this is a matter of a crisis and a matter of enormous urgency. Precedents have been cited to the effect that there have been many studies made on the matter of food prices by this House, the other place and by the two places combined. This also leads me to believe the whole matter of food prices is an extremely complex and difficult one, that we really cannot study the whole matter of the rise in food prices within a very short time and make any real analysis of what causes this part of our economy go off kilter every once in a while or, as most housewives would indicate, go off kilter most of the time.
Usually this House and the country is enjoined by the members of the Progressive Conservative party-and here I speak traditionally and historically-to proceed with caution. Surely, it is the function of a Conservative group to advise the nation that care must be taken and haste made but made slowly. Yesterday, however, we heard there was a crisis at hand and heard accusations from the Tory benches to the effect that the government has been doing nothing and that action is needed. Mind you, in all these calls for action there have been no specific suggestions concerning what kind of action should be taken, so what we see now in this House is a shift in the Progressive Conservative "mot d'ordre". It is not a matter of making haste slowly but doing nothing swiftly. One may be allowed to suspect that the Tories-I am not talking about motives but rather reasons-have unspoken reasons for having the study of this very complex matter completed within three months. I just may be that the kind of action they are urging on the government, properly defined, is a form of inaction and that really what they want is that there be nothing done on this whole question but that it be done with dispatch.
Last night the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) read us a rather dreary list of people in the other place who have overt and open connections with the 25714-31
Food Prices Committee
food industry in Canada. I am sure that if we were to project this list a little further we would find many members of the loyal opposition who also have direct and indirect interests in the food industry in Canada.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: And on the other side.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
We will get to the other side eventually. I think what we really need to do is change the approach of this committee in such a way that it will be able to pursue the matter in depth and not be a nine-day or three-month wonder of a committee but rather a committee which will be able to solve a problem which has been besetting this country for a long time. It is a problem which has been facing every household with intensity. For this reason at least, we must charge this committee with the need to report to this House and to the nation this winter, particularly on some of the worst aspects and abuses of the pricing system in Canada.
It is not necessary to have a committee of this House to tell the average Canadian housewife that a good part of the price she pays for food must be attributable to the excessive cost of advertising. In my city of Toronto one day a week the great dailies publish enormous advertising sections detailing in print and in picture for the benefit of the poor housewife exactly what a roast of beef looks like. She would be quite satisfied with a simple little list printed in a certain part of the paper collating the prices of the various cuts of meat and various other foodstuffs store by store, and supermarket by supermarket. She has to plough through reams and reams of print and pages and pages of pictures which very often at best could be said to be misleading in respect of the actual economies she would receive if she pursued the urging of the advertisement. Certainly at that level a committee of inquiry such as we are discussing in this House could act very quickly. This is a problem which is obvious to practically everybody in this country, if not to every member in this House.
What we have before us is a very complex problem. It is one which is deep-rooted and which goes into the very nature of the production and distributive system in this country. At the same time, there are aspects of the problem which any person with any common sense could tell us are subject to immediate action. If we subscribe to the amendment from the Progressive Conservative benches proposed by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) not only would we be running the risk of doing nothing but would also be running the concomitant risk, to use his own words, of damaging one very important sector of our nation. Members of my party yesterday made the very important point that this House must not act swiftly to the point of detrimentally affecting the interests of the basic producers in this country. The people in this country who stand to lose the most and be hurt the most by hasty action on the whole question of the price of food, food production and distribution are the basic producers, the farmers of this country. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) pointed out, it is only recently that they have begun to receive something like a part of the kind of price they should have been receiving a long time ago.

January 19, 1973
Food Prices Committee
Another sector of our nation and our economy that we should be careful not to hurt is those who are involved as workers in the packing and processing industries. Yesterday, I think someone in the House quoted the figure of $6 an hour with reference to workers working in the food processing industry. It is almost impossible, when looking at the statistics produced by Statistics Canada, to know exactly what it is that a food packer or processor receives on the average, but I can assure you from my knowledge of what food processors receive in Toronto that it is a long way from $6 an hour. So, there we have another very important segment of the food producing, processing and distributing industry in Canada which would be extremely vulnerable to hasty, inconsiderate action on the part of the House.
There are other reasons for not asking this committee to move to completion of its work within three months. The other reasons are of a much more positive nature than the ones I have just outlined. Many of us feel that there is something that is in need of a drastic change in the whole matter of food producing and distributing in this country. Many of us feel, too, that no matter what specific recommendations we put forward to change what now exists, we will have somehow failed if we do not start thinking and recommending other ways in which the whole matter of food distribution can be handled. For example, we have had attempts, some successful and some unsuccessful, in various communities in Canada to establish consumer based or indeed community based distribution systems for foodstuffs and household needs. We have seen in Halifax, for example, the successful establishment of a direct charge co-operative. We have seen a similar successful establishment in Hamilton, and there is an excellent one in Oshawa which has been able to establish and maintain itself successfully, mainly because it has had the effective backing of a very large and community sensitive part of that locality, that is the United Auto Workers.
Again, we can say that the case was more or less the same in Hamilton. If United Steel Workers of America had not supported fully the direct charge co-op in operation there, one could be allowed to wonder whether it would have moved at all. The direct charge co-op idea is a new idea in food distribution, not only in this country but in the whole of North America. It provides for a lot of excellent aspects. It provides, in effect, for real consumer control over the quantity, quality and pricing of the products that are put on the shelves. It provides for a very direct understanding on the part of consumers of exactly what goes into the pricing of the products they buy after the society gets the products from the wholesalers. It provides for a new establishment of confidence on the part of the consumer in the whole mechanism of distribution, because he feels he has some control over it and he begins to understand exactly why prices do go up in certain cases. It certainly provides for something which is extremely valuable and necessary in so many of our communities, and that is yet another way among the many needed ways to build up a sense of community among our people and to eliminate the alienation that so many of our citizens feel about the whole process by which this country is governed. Alienation among the citizens exists not

only with regard to the political process but also with regard to private enterprise which is supposed to support society's basic economy and satisfy its basic needs.
So, it would be very important for this committee to look into these positive areas to see what this House could do to help Canadians establish institutions, vending and supply institutions in which they would participate, institutions which they would control. There has been some talk in the past few years of participatory democracy, and a lot of it has been very much like the talk we have heard about the need for action. It has been action but no specifics, and participate but no specifics. We have here a very real case of citizens of this country, as consumers, participating in establishing at least a part of the economic democracy which we all wish to see established eventually.
Because there is a real need to go into this matter of food pricing in depth, and because there is a real need for this House to take action in some of the more immediate areas which are more susceptible to correction, such as the matter of advertising-and I have given the House simply one example-and because there is again a very real need for the House to inspect new areas of positive action to allow the Canadian consumer more real control over the economic conditions which he has to face every week as a consumer, and because there is a real need for the House to consider ways in which the government of this country could aid the citizens of this country establish their forms of economic democratic participation in the way that trade unions in this country have done, I would like to move an amendment modifying the amendment put forward by the hoft. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath).
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes):
That the amendment be amended by deleting the words "within the three months next following its appointment", and by substituting therefor the following words: "upon the completion of its investigation, and that it shall make an interim report, including recommendations for action, within two months of its first meeting".
The clause as amended would then read as follows:
That the said committee shall make its final report and recommendations upon the completion of its investigation, and that it shall make an interim report, including recommendations for action, within two months of its first meeting.

Mr. Speaker, since this is the first occasion which I have had to speak in the chamber in this particular session I want to express, along with others in the House, my congratulations to Mr. Speaker. It was my good fortune to be a member during the twenty-eighth parliament, and we found that all we had heard about Mr. Speaker at that time was most assuredly true. He conducted himself with dignity and, happily, with a great sense of humour.
I think, however, that the appointment which pleased me even more was your appointment, Sir, as Deputy Speaker because at long last the government had caught up with a proposition that I had made in the last House when we had a majority. At that time, I broke the rule by
January 19, 1973

voting in the Committee on Veterans Affairs to appoint Mr. Chester MacRae, then Member of Parliament, as vice chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. So, the government has seen the wisdom of the step I took at that time. Since the government made that decision, I do not think it could have found a more appropriate member from Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition to appoint to that high position. I also wish to pay my compliments very briefly to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. As one who had that happy experience in 1969,1 can assure them that it is an honour they will cherish long after they have left this establishment.

Mr. Speaker, last night the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) said, as reported on page 454 of Hansard, and I quote:
Senator Robichaud who is involved in National Sea Products Ltd.
The Hon. Gerard Robichaud is no longer senator; he is Lieutenant-Governor of New Brunswick. Let us get our facts straight.

Hon. members will be happy to hear that that is the extent of my contribution to this debate in French.
No one can dispute that food costs are rising. It is a fact that is most familiar to those who are on fixed incomes, particularly our senior citizens. Most assuredly it is familiar to all of us to one degree or another. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) suggest that the government in some way was endeavouring to sweep the problem under the rug. I would remind him that it was the government which proposed this measure, pointing out that food costs are rising, and urging that a committee should study food costs to see what action can be taken to stop the rise in food prices. It is my hope that the committee can do just that.
But having criticized the setting up of the committee, and having suggested that it will sweep the problem under the rug, what constructive comment did we hear from him on how to make the committee work? Mr. Speaker, the official opposition seem to be more content to move from newspaper headline to newspaper headline than to make this house work as the people of Canada want it to work. Who is to blame? That is the question that is constantly asked with respect to food prices. The issue is not easy to determine. We have heard a recital of the series of committees and commissions that were established to see if something could be done to halt rising food prices. The last committee we established recommended the establishment of a department of consumer affairs, and that recommendation came to fruition as a result of action taken by a Liberal government. It is not correct to say that committee reports are only put on a shelf to gather dust. That committee made a recommendation, and the recommendation was accepted by the government. Today, we have the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
The next step was the establishment of the Prices and Incomes Commission by the Department of Consumer
25714-31)
Food Prices Committee
and Corporate Affairs. That commission was subjected to a great deal of criticism, but the criticism generated more heat than light. The commission fulfilled a definite function, a necessary function, at the time it was established. It pointed out to consumers that there were areas where people could curb the rise in wages, in prices and in incomes, also rises in salaries at the federal, provincial and municipal level. It pointed out the problems and the need for us, in this time of affluence, to show some form of restraint. In my view-

speechtext:
Order. The Chair finds itself in difficulty because, with the amendment and the subamendment, the compass of the debate is really very narrow. This works a hardship on members, such as the hon. member now speaking, who is delivering his general thoughts on this whole topic rather than confining himself to the question of whether there should be an interim report, including recommendations for action, within two months of the first meeting of the committee. Because of the rules of the House, that is precisely the confines of the debate.
I do not want to be overly strict because that would only prompt two speeches from the hon. member, one dealing with that particular point, and then one later on dealing with his general approach. This is something that might be given consideration before we meet again at two o'clock, to see whether the house leaders are agreed that the vote should be on Monday so that we may consider that we are on the general debate rather than on the particular amendment and subamendment. I really am in difficulty, and since we are starting off a new parliament it is rather important that we adhere to the usual practice.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Your Honour, may I make a comment on your very proper observation that if the speakers were to be held strictly to the amendment and subamendment it would indeed be a very narrow debate? Probably under the strict application of the rules of relevancy that ought to be the case, but it seems to me that from time to time we have overlooked the rules of relevancy, and no more recently than yesterday when the amendment before the House was upon the question of removal of the Senate from the proposed committee. At that time, most of the speeches were of a very general character and only touched tagentially on the question of Senate participation. I suggest that as a matter of agreement by the House, without asking you to associate yourself with any deterioration in the application of the rules, we might agree to allow the debate to be of a general character on all these subamendments that may come along today and later. That is the first point I want to make.
The second point I want to make is that I understand that it is not likely there will be a vote today. Certainly, I am operating on the assumption that there will not be a vote on either the subamendment of the amendment today. For that reason, this does provide an opportunity for members to talk generally. I hope these observations may be of some help to the Chair.

speechtext: Order. I think the Chair gathers the mood of the House. I would have to agree with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) that this matter did not just erupt this morning, and that there were very wide ranging speeches yesterday. Before giving the floor again to the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), I wish to assure him that the time spent on this point will not be taken from his allocation of time. I also wish to apologize to him for raising the matter in the middle of this speech, in view of the fact that it could have been raised during speeches given in the House yesterday.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I certainly do not feel put upon because I was interrupted. It gave me an opportunity to catch my breath and ask a Page for a glass of water. I was speaking first in a general vein because I thought this was necessary before going on to deal with the amendment and the subamendment. I think that the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney) is a good one. It points out that the committee has an obligation at the beginning to do all it can within a two month period. If it can make recommendations that is well and good, and we can have an interim report. We will have to look at the involvement of governments, labour unions, farmers, supermarkets and that mysterious fellow, the middleman. But to attempt all this with a time limitation of three months does not seem to make much sense if the committee is to have any meaning at all. It seems to me that we need more time, but I think we can come up with an interim report.
Criticisms are often directed at farmers, at unions, at supermarkets and governments as well as other people. Much of this criticism has no basis in fact, and the charges are too often made from ignorance of the facts. A charge is often made against a government purely for political gain or by a consumer out of frustration and because he does not know the facts. That is why we need this committee and why it has to last longer than three months-why it will last longer than three months. Mr. Speaker, that is why I find the subamendment one which I can support.
If the committee is to be limited to the three-months period, it will be natural enough that the favourite target will be the government. It is always easy to establish a common bond against the government on almost any issue. The next favourite target is the supermarket moguls, they are fair game in our society. They are also adept at answering criticism and need no defence from me in this chamber. The thing that makes me happy is that less and less criticism is directed against the farmers. It seems that the farmers are getting their message across.

The new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has for many years been the champion of farmers. It must be very rewarding to hold a portfolio which gives the widest possible audience, in defence of and in appreciation of farmers. He is still at the same old stand, notwithstanding his new responsibilities.
I was extremely pleased to read the speech the minister made in Halifax in which he again put it to the farmers that they must get their message across and that they have an obligation to use the manpower services. This is the sort of thing that farmers will be reminded of when they come before the committee. In that speech, referred to in the remarks of the hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), according to the minister, when people were getting a bargain on food prices they were getting a bargain as far as the farmers were concerned, that farmers have had increased their productivity and so the Canadian consumer was getting a good deal. The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham should read the speech again and not take a sentence out of context, suggesting that the minister might be indicating that prices were not on the rise. The minister was simply indicating that in these circumstances the farmer is not to blame.
Mr. Speaker, bearing in mind your admonition, I am going to limit my remarks. I feel that the debate should not become too wide because we will have an opportunity before the committee to go into the many different aspects of this subject. I hope that we will see representatives of the Consumer Association of Canada before this committee. They have done a tremendous amount of research on this subject, and to confine the committee to a three-month period would do a disservice to them and others like them. They will need a good deal of time in order to present the results of their research to the committee. The supermarkets will also need time to establish their position before the committee. If profits are exorbitant, then the committee will have an obligation to say so in its report; if it is felt that controls are necessary then the committee should make that recommendation, bearing in mind, of course, that where there is a shortage of food, controls will not get at the basic issue. I hope that senior citizens will also appear before the committee to explain their difficulties. Perhaps they could show the young lady of today the proper way to shop as they have unhappily learned out of necessity. Perhaps a new horizons program is necessary.
I have been told by a lady who made a serious study of this, that by checking the newspaper ads, by listening to the radio as I do myself on my way to work-on Thursday mornings, CBO has a commentator who gives comparable meat prices and tells where the best bargains are-and by studying nutrition magazines, she found that she could feed her family better and save about $10 a week on her food bill. Consumers have an obligation to take that kind of action rather than to indulge a preference for prepackaged and prepared foods as seems to be the case in this day and age. If price is no object or if they can afford the luxury, more power to them, but there are many people who should be looking very carefully at their shopping lists and they should be able to appear before the committee.
January 19, 1973

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney). As a backbencher, I cannot speak on behalf of my party, but it seems to me that the subamendment makes good sense and is fair to the consumers of Canada. The supermarket operators, government representatives, the farmers, the unions and anyone else who wishes to appear before that committee should have the opportunity. I hope that this committee will make a serious attempt to solve the extremely difficult problem of rising food prices.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the advantages of having a colleague from one's province in the chair is that he knows the name of one's constituency. This is appreciated, especially in my case, when my constituency became part of the former constituency of Colchester-Hants. As a result, I was often addressed as the hon. member for Northumber-land-Colchester-Hants but with Your Honour in the chair I am now correctly known as the member for Cumberland-Colchester North.
Since this is the first time I have participated in debate in this parliament, I should like to offer to you, Sir, my congratulations in public as I have in private. I know that you will honour the position for which you have been chosen by all members of this House and I anticipate great things from you in the days ahead.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) and, to a degree, appreciated what he said. I think all members of this House have an understanding of the problem that we face, the problem of spiralling costs, especially food costs. These increases make it difficult for anyone on a fixed income, and especially those living below the poverty level, to go into the supermarket and purchase foods in keeping with their income. They know and we know that this is important. Every day that goes by the task of making the dollar meet requirements is more difficult. We, as a party, are somewhat hesistant about endorsing the approach that the government has adopted in order to try to combat the problem.
The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) has pointed out why we are hesitant, why we are somewhat doubtful about the government's approach. While we believe that the matter is urgent, we do not believe that it will be solved by a committee. I agree, in part with what the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) was saying on this subject. He suggested, as did the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), that the report should not be made in three months because everyone who wishes to appear before the committee should be given the opportunity of having a say. Parliamentary committees and other committees established by governments to sit for a certain time usually exceed the time limit allocated to them before presenting a report. That limit is exceeded sometimes on two or three occasions. There are indications that this procedure has become the rule rather than the exception.
Food Prices Committee
I am also concerned about parliamentary committees being democratic committees. Anyone who wants to appear before the committee should, as the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton suggested, be given the opportunity to say something. If this is what is wanted, in my opinion the other place should set up its own committee. It should travel across the country and, keeping in mind the long range point of view, secure the advice and opinion of all who want to appear before it. Then, that committee could produce a long range proposal somewhat similar to the report of the committee established by the other place on aging or on land use. I could assist the government in that way.
I think the consumer of this country is fed up with complaining. This committee will merely listen to complaints. It will travel from coast to coast and listen to people say what is wrong with this and that, and how the price of this and that has risen. What the consumer wants is action, Mr. Speaker, and not more reports, submissions and arguments as to who is at fault. Whether you like it or not, the administration of this country is at fault because prices are skyrocketing and it has not taken the necessary action to stop it. If this government is not capable of taking that action, if it has not formulated a plan, as it ought to have, to contain costs realistically, it should move out of the way and make room for somebody else who can do the job. I think my party could do it. I think my party ought to be in office now, and certainly this is the opinion of the electors of this country.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Certainly, if they were given the opportunity tomorrow to indicate which party they prefer to run the affairs of this nation, they would indicate the party I support. Let me present evidence for my statement. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) said on January 18, as recorded in Hansard at page 431:
In statistical terms the increase in food prices from December 1971 to December 1972 was 8.6 per cent. Over the same period, the rise for all items other than food in the consumer price index was 3.8 per cent.
I do not argue with what the minister says. If he says that, I am sure he is right. On the same date, as reported in the Globe and Mail, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) made a speech in Halifax to members of Canada's dairy industry. The report of that Speech reads:
Mr. Whelan feels the public must be conditioned to expect to pay a more realistic price for food. An average Canadian wage earner is paying less proportionately of his income for food now, than he was 10 years ago,... If food costs had risen in the same proportion as the rest of the consumer price index items, beef farmers would now be getting 70 cents a pound for beef on the hoof, rather than 40 cents.
Then, the minister is reported to have said:
I think we should be telling consumers what a fine job we have been doing, and what a bargain they are getting.
You can have it one way or the other, Mr. Speaker, not both ways. Either consumer food prices are going up faster than other prices, as the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs suggests, or they are not, as the Minister of Agriculture suggests. The report continues:

January 19, 1973
Food Prices Committee
Mr. Whelan said nobody seems to complain about increases in the price of beer, furs, snowmobiles and other luxuries. You don't hear a peep out of them. But if a couple of cents are added to food costs everybody is screaming.
I do not know what the Minister of Agriculture thinks, but I am not too greatly concerned about people who are buying snowmobiles, furs and other luxuries. Perhaps they are not screaming, for good reason. But the great majority of people in this country are screaming because food prices are going up and they just do not have money to buy food. Previous to the October 30 election, we underwent four and a half years of the present administration. What did we get from it? We got nothing for those on fixed incomes; they were not compensated for increases in living costs. That is why those people are screaming about increases in costs of food and consumer items. They do not have money in their pockets to buy those things. With the dollars left in their pockets they cannot buy sufficient food today to maintain their families. We must do something about that.
We can do something in several ways: First, by increasing the various types of federal pensions, thus giving certain people sufficient income to meet increases in living costs; second, by gearing those pensions to the cost of living increase; and, third, by controlling the sorts of increases that are being imposed everywhere at the present time in this country. May I call it one o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPOINT SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Order, please. It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock.
At one o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was making some general statements about the committee that is proposed and some of the areas in which it might work. I wish to again refer to the comments of the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton, with regard to comparative consumer reports that are sometimes of value to food buyers. In that regard, it might be of some value to a consumer to know the comparative values in the various supermarkets when purchasing a certain item. However, it does not help very much when that item in all supermarkets has increased by 10 per cent or 20 per cent in one week. This does occur. I have encountered it.
I wish to make specific mention of two items which I purchased in a grocery store over a very short period of time. They both were significantly increased in price. One of these was a food item. I purchased this for 77 cents and, two or three weeks later, I paid 98 cents for this same item. That really shakes up a person. That is the type of increase that so-called discount operators are providing for consumers. Another item that came to my attention this past weekend was fuses. When I removed the last fuse from a container of three in my home, I noticed that the price on it was 22 cents. When I went to the food store to purchase a replacement, the price was 41 cents for three

fuses. I do not know how long I had the first three fuses I referred to, but in was not a long period of time. In that period of time, the price had jumped almost 100 per cent. This is the sad situation that has been facing consumers all across this country.
There may be many areas the committee will have to study in order to determine what might be done to assist the purchasing public. One basic problem, certainly in Atlantic Canada and probably across the country, is the spiralling cost of feed concentrates to producers to be included in products destined for grocery stores, certainly in so far as meat is concerned. On November 20,1 wrote a letter to the Minister of Agriculture similar to one I had written some time before to the former Minister of Transport. In that letter, I pointed out the unbelievable increases producers in the Atlantic provinces must pay for feed grains. I quote from my November 30 letter:
The cost of feed additives has increased substantially. It is my understanding that the increase in the cost of soybean meal has been $55.00 per ton for meat meal and fish meal, the increase has been approximately $50.00 per ton.
In so far as feed grains are concerned, as of October 23rd, barley has increased in price from $8.00 to $10.00 per ton, corn is up $12.00 per ton, No. 5 feed wheat is up $10.50 per ton, oats are up $14.00 to $15.00 per ton, mill feeds are up as much as $22.00 per ton, and hog grower and hog finisher are up $6.00 per ton.
There is no way the farmers of this country can stand that type of increase without receiving additional payment for their products. Unless there is something this government can do to assist the farmers, they will have to add on this cost to the price of their products. This has been happening over and over again. From the time that increase in cost goes from the producer to the purchaser, it is hard to believe how much of an increase the person buying that product has to pay. Certainly only a small portion of that goes into the pocket of the farmer who is trying to maintain a livelihood in extremely difficult circumstances. I also suggested to the Minister of Agriculture that as far as feed concentrates were concerned, there should be special action taken by the government that would be of material assistance to the farmers of Atlantic Canada.
I wish to put on record a resolution that was passed by the Maritime Farmers Council. This is a federation which includes the New Brunswick Federation of Agriculture, the Maritime Co-operative Services, the Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture and the Prince Edward Island Confederation of Agriculture. Their resolution on feed concentrates reads as follows:
Whereas animal and vegetable protein concentrates constitute approximately 13 per cent of hog feed rations, 15 per cent of broiler feed rations and 9 per cent of layer rations, and
Whereas the price of all animal and vegetable protein concentrates is governed by the price of soybean meal, and
Whereas during the past five months the cost of soybean meal has increased by more than 60 per cent from $140 per ton to $225 per ton, basis f.o.b. Moncton; with similar increases in other protein concentrates, and
Whereas this is causing an increase of $4.25 in the cost of producing a market hog, with similar increases in livestock, dairy and poultry production, and
January 19, 1973

Whereas this represents an intolerable situation when combined with rising costs of feed grains, transportation, and other production input expenses, and
Whereas even at the greatly increased price there is a real danger that the supply of protein concentrates made available may not be sufficient to support our livestock and poultry industries,
Therefore be it resolved that we urge the federal government to authorize the Canadian Livestock Feed Board to buy soybean meal and/or other protein concentrates, and position these ingredients for our use, and
Be it further resolved that we ask that the price for these concentrates be protected at $130 per ton, basis f.o.b. carlot Toronto, for soybean meal.
If that action were taken, the purchasing public would have a substantial guarantee that there would not be the increases in food prices they are now facing. Everybody would enjoy some stability in the market place, and in the result there would be less inflation in this nation. Whether or not the committee hears complaints from people about food prices, this action is required in order to get some stability and end the spiral of inflation for an unprotected purchasing public. Whether the committee sits or does not sit, whether these facts are laid before the committee or not, the price of food will continue to go up and up and up without a corresponding increase in the amount of money in the pockets of Canadians to buy that food.
In the province of Nova Scotia, families are asked under the provincial social assistance scheme-

speechtext: Order. I regret I have to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him under the House order passed yesterday has expired. He can continue with unanimous consent.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North.

Mr. Speaker, I can finish in a couple of sentences, and 1 thank the House for its courtesy in allowing me to continue. I was saying that under the social assistance plan in Nova Scotia, families are asked to try to maintain themselves, no matter what their size, on $200 a month. This means that people are going to starve to death under this spiralling increase in the cost of living.
We believe, and rightly so, that any committee of the House that is established to study food prices must get the job done quickly and report back within the shortest possible period of time. I think that three months, in itself, is almost too long; we should be taking action today. If we were the party forming the government of this country today, the people would get action today. But under the present government the people will have to wait at least three months. And the government is saying that three months is not long enough. It may not be enough for this government, but for many people who are trying to survive on next to nothing it is the devil of a long time. People are going to have a mighty hard winter if they have to wait for the committee to sit. It seems obvious from the comments that have come forth from government benches since the amendment was introduced that the government is not even satisfied with three months. They want the people to wait even longer for some remedy to
Food Prices Committee
their problem. It may be these people will no longer be on this earth when the government finally does take action on their behalf.

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been paying close attention to this debate, which has been one of the more interesting debates. Speeches by individual members have been of high quality. However, I am afraid that the speeches particularly from members of the official opposition, have been very good in histrionics but very poor in terms of content.
The question is simply this. We are faced in the world today with spiralling prices. Such a condition is not unique to Canada. We do not have the highest rate of inflation or the highest increase in prices of any country in the world. Countries are doing worse than we are, and there are even a few who are doing better. But it is obvious that there is no easy answer.
I think all of us on this side of the House would have been impressed had the hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), who admittedly is a new member in the House, been able to indicate exactly what was Tory policy. But there is no Tory policy, and this is why, to illustrate the poverty of their thought, hon. members opposite had to steal the sheets from the bed of the NDP.
That is the bed you are in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Sheets that the Liberals have soiled.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: After last night I hope they enjoyed their one night of bliss. I hope the NDP enjoyed it, too. Perhaps they will find that the "official" opposition are not their only bedmates.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: They have already discovered that you are economically impotent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not blame the hon. member for North-umberland-Durham for the kind of speech he made yesterday. It is something that we in this particular parliament have come to expect from the Tory benches-in other words, nothing. After all, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham is merely following in the steps of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who had nothing to offer in terms of policy when he spoke in the throne speech debate. He was quite upset that the NDP looked at his speech and decided it contained nothing. That is why the NDP preferred to go along with the government, which has offered something concrete, a plan for action in the future. This is why the NDP has not supported the Tories. The NDP do not particularly like the government, and they do not particularly like hon. members opposite; but hon. members on that side have not even given the NDP anything to hang on to in order to encourage them to vote against us.
The attitude of the official opposition can be likened to that of the big bad wolf in the famous story who was going to huff and puff and blow the house down. They have certainly let out a lot of hot air; but the only time they have been able to get any support in the House, outside of their own, was when they borrowed the bed-

January 19, 1973
Food Prices Committee
sheets from the bed of the NDP and moved a motion that one would normally have expected the NDP to move, since the party has a long history of being opposed to the Senate. We were not aware that the Conservative party had suddenly changed its view overnight.
The idea they borrowed from the NDP was not even germane to the motion that was before the House. I think we can offer the official opposition a bit of advice. If they are really serious about defeating the government and want to come over on this side, they are not going to accomplish that objective with hot air. It is not going to be achieved by speeches such as that of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, or even by a speech like that of the hon. Leader of the Opposition during the throne speech debate. This can only be achieved by substantive policy recommendations. When hon. members really start to deal with the nitty-gritty issues facing this country today, then members on this side of the House may start to fear for their seats. When they start to do these things, then we will begin to have a debate in this House that is meaningful. We might then have debate in the House that will attract the attention of the ordinary person in Canada. Until that time, I am afraid this House of Commons is not going to attract that kind of attention.
Tell us the price of beef; you have not mentioned that yet.
Question, question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I know the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) is enjoying the attention he is attracting, but the difficulty is that under our ancient practices the Chair is supposed to hear at least some of the speech which is now being interrupted. I would ask that the hon. member be allowed to continue without the number of interventions that have been taking place.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I say that we thoroughly agree with you, and we hope the hon. member will say something that we think is at least worth hearing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thank you very much for your intervention, Mr. Speaker, but I do not really fear that those hon. members opposite who have been yelling and screaming during my rather quiet remarks have been able to divert me from my purpose, which is to discuss some of the issues before us. I would like to direct some remarks to the amendment and the sub-amendment which have been moved.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The previous speaker indicated he felt the committee ought to complete its deliberations within a three month period. As former chairman of a committee, I have always taken the attitude that when a committee is given something to do it ought to have a time limit of some kind and ought to be under a greater degree of control by the House. However, it seems to me that to expect any group of hon. members in the House of Commons to look into the totality of factors that affect food prices in

Canada within a short period of time is unrealistic. I think a far better proposition could be made, that the committee should be instructed to make substantive reports to the House of Commons from time to time in order that we might keep a running check on its activities and control more precisely what the committee is doing. Speaking for myself and not the government, I would think some form of amendment which indicated that we wanted the committee to report on an interim basis, say once every two or three months, would be acceptable to me as an individual and, I think, would be given serious consideration by the minister.
We all recognize that committee members become very much wrapped up in their own activities and do not spend much time following the will of the House. Sometimes they even substitute their own desires for those of the House. Because of the complexities involved in the factors surrounding food prices, it is not fair to force upon any group of men, even those from the opposition, a time limit within which they must produce a final and definitive report. That simply is not realistic.
You are weaseling now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: One has only to examine the factors involved in food prices to understand the point I am trying to make.
Quick action is what we need from this government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) says we need quick action. What quick action did his party ever propose? One has only to read his leader's speech on the throne speech debate or the speech of the lead-off speaker for his party to find out that nothing is proposed. I suggest that is what the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi stands for, nothing.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say that with apologies to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander).
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are a number of items the committee must consider, one being that the increasing amount of food we consume today is not in the form of raw agricultural produce. Instead, we are eating much more processed food. When we purchase food, we are not purchasing the raw product in many cases but products subjected to a high degree of ^processing. In terms of volume alone last year in the United States there were more potatoes processed into frozen french fries and, goodness knows what other kinds, than sold in their natural state. The trend is probably the same in Canada.
We are dealing with a system in which people are demanding a higher degree of processing and, therefore, paying a higher price than would be paid for the product in its natural state. I suggest there are reasons for this situation. There has been a substantial change in the life style of Canadians within the last 10 or 15 years. Let us take the example of a man and wife who are both working. When they come home after a hard day's work they
January 19, 1973

want a meal which can be prepared with a minimum of strain. They buy frozen meals, frozen french fried potatoes and other frozen products, all of which require a great deal of processing and the expenditure of a considerable amount of money. If people make that choice, are they really paying a higher price for food than they might had they purchased it in the natural state, or are they making a choice as to the disposition of the moneys they have left over after paying for necessities? This involves a question not so much of food prices but of how people spend their discretionary incomes.
In the last two or three months I have been making a tour of my constituency and interviewing a lot of small grocery store operators.
What is discretionary about a price tag?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If a person wants to buy frozen potatoes instead of table potatoes and has to spend three times as much, is not that person making a discretionary purchase? I suggest that he is because he has a choice as to how he will spend his money for food.
What choice has he got?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the price of potatoes in their natural state were going up as fast as the price of potatoes in the processed state I would say we should really be concerned, but that is not the case.
You are never concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: One merely has.to read the speech of the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) and other members who represent agricultural constituencies who spoke during this debate to learn that this is not so. Farmers are not making that much money, because farm prices are low. It is not the farmer who is making the money, it is the processor, the people who have caused this product to be in demand are the consumers who also have the opportunity of buying the product in its natural state. The consumer is spending his discretionary income, and apparently that is satisfactory. That is the simple point I wanted to make, and I think the hon. member now understands it.
Thank you for making it, but how many months did it take you to come to that conclusion?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are dealing with a society in which the life style has changed. We find ourselves in a situation in which we have added more links in the chain that brings the food from the farmer, through the processor, the wholesaler and the retailer to the consumer.
Before I was interrupted, I was talking about having interviews with people who operate small grocery stores in my constituency. They told me there were a number of reasons for the increase in prices last year. One individual told me quite bluntly that a substantial part of the increase over the last six months could be attributed to politicians.

Hear, hear!
Food Prices Committee

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was a little shocked by this statement. He said that a substantial part of this increase could be attributed to politicians who have been talking about the imposition of wage and price controls. As a result these companies, in order to protect themselves, increased the prices in case that event came about. It is difficult to say whether there is truth in that suggestion. If there is, there is a lesson for us to learn. We should be careful of what we are saying to those people who might actually believe that some of the members of this House are serious.
Well, you are innocent. You have not talked about wage and price controls.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The committee must consider the sociological factors. Most members have not bothered to mention this aspect.
The committee must also consider questions in relation to long-term food supply. I have been reading a book called "The Limits of Growth" in which the Club of Rome and MIT computer studies indicate that no matter what is done in terms of decreasing population through birth control, and increasing the supply of food through the use of non-arable land that might be exploited, and increasing the yield from land now under cultivation, there is no way we can meet the challenge to produce enough food to feed the estimated population of the next 30 years.
This year we have had reports of the beginning of famine in the new country of Bangladesh and in India. We have seen the prices for food increase across the world simply because there seems to be a shortage. The hon. member who spoke before me mentioned the substantial increase in the price of feed grains. He would probably be interested to know that last fall the United States removed all quotas in order to encourage the import of beef and other meat products into the United States because of a scarcity in that type of protein. He would also be interested to know that the country perhaps most noted for tariffs, France, was also faced with a shortage of protein and removed its 7 i per cent value added tax recently. So, countries are attempting to cope with this shortage by removing tariffs and destroying the protection they built up in respect of their food industries. This indicates that the problem is not solely a Canadian one but is worldwide, not only in the long-term but also in the short-term.
It was interesting to me to note that, in applying its wage and price controls, the United States specifically decided to exclude raw agricultural products although these controls were applied to other products of the manufacturing sector of the food industry in that country. Unfortunately, even though my hon. friends across the way deny it, there really is no easy solution to the problem. Canada, as an international trading nation with 25 per cent of its gross national product based on foreign trade, and one job in five based on foreign trade, will not be immune to these inflationary factors which are outside our control. We try to operate in an international economy and must do so. There are certain consequences which fall upon us. It seems to me that the problems of inflation which beset not only Canada and the United States but the world as a whole, are not solvable at the local level but
486

Food Prices Committee
rather on an international level. It is a brutal fact of life that we do not have sovereignty over a number of things which affect us and our living standards. It has always been Canadian policy to try to work through international organizations such as FAO, the United Nations and the Group of Ten in an effort to solve problems common to all. I suggest this is a problem which will find its solution, not in the deliberations of this House of Commons but in the deliberations of worldwide bodies.
Now, I should like to come to the point related to the question of nutrition. In the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River there were four candidates during the last election. There was myself, the Conservative candidate, the NDP candidate and an independent candidate. The independent candidate ran on the platform of a guaranteed annual income as well as the matter of nutrition. The point he tried to make in that election campaign was that the nutrition value of the food we buy is not as good as it should be, and that there are other ways in which to acquire the nutrition our bodies need. The federal government has sponsored a nutrition study to find out how well Canadians are being fed and how well they choose their food from what is available as well as how well that food is actually prepared in order to keep the nutritional value intact. The preliminary reports of that study are not particularly encouraging, because the indication is that many Canadians do not take advantage of the nutritional value of the food we now have. Perhaps an anecodote will illustrate the point.
When talking to a grocer I asked him about the nutritional value of many foods, particularly prepared foods, and he said that the greatest tragedy-

Agreed.
